discovery: Quantum key distribution: the invention of quantum cryptography and its foundation in quantum measurement and entanglement

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) showed that the disturbance caused by measuring a quantum system, long seen as a limitation, can guarantee the secrecy of a shared key. This was the first protocol whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. Ekert (E91) linked key distribution to entanglement and Bell inequalities, turning the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations tested experimentally in the 1980s into a resource whose non-local character certifies security. That insight led to device-independent cryptography. Together these works founded quantum communication. They inspired four decades of experiments with single photons, entangled pairs and continuous-variable coherent states, and they led to metropolitan networks, satellite links and commercial systems. They clarified what quantum measurement really implies and turned the foundational questions honoured in 2022 into practical technology. This is exactly the kind of lasting contribution the Prize should recognise.
